![A classroom scene illustrating the 1:1 device era. Image from [The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2026/05/07/states-limit-school-screen-time/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

Lauren Lumpkin, [reporting for *The Washington Post*](https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2026/05/07/states-limit-school-screen-time/), walks through the ed-tech pullback underway in U.S. K–12.

What the article reports:

- **Pandemic-era spending.** Districts spent between $15 billion and $35 billion of federal pandemic relief between 2020 and 2024 on laptops, tablets, and learning software, per an [Edunomics Lab](https://edunomicslab.org/) estimate. By last school year, [a federal survey](https://ies.ed.gov/learn/press-release/more-half-public-school-leaders-say-cell-phones-hurt-academic-performance) found 88 percent of public schools had given every child a device.
- **Pullback underway.** At least a dozen states introduced or adopted policies this year to regulate in-school screen time. Parent groups such as Schools Beyond Screens are pushing districts to roll back 1:1 device rollouts.
- **State-level policy shapes.** Utah's state board is banning screen time for most K–3 subjects. Iowa capped elementary digital instruction at 60 minutes a day. A Missouri bill would require every district to set a screen-time policy.
- **Beyond minutes per day.** [Curriculum Associates](https://www.curriculumassociates.com/) is facing a lawsuit over alleged unauthorized collection of student data via its i-Ready platform. YouTube, allowed in classrooms because teachers use it for instruction, is cited as a persistent source of distraction.
- **Thin research base.** A meta-analysis of reading-comprehension studies finds paper beats digital. A [new NBER paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35132) released this week finds in-school cellphone bans had little effect on academic outcomes.

One line from the piece, by Missouri state Rep. Tricia Byrnes:

> Ed tech is just big tech in a sweater vest.

## My Notes

- **The ed-tech thesis assumed content delivery was the bottleneck. It wasn't.** Districts bought laptops and learning software expecting infinite personalized practice to move outcomes. What's missing is the layer around the content that turns "access to material" into "engagement with material": a teacher calling on a student by name, a grade that matters, peer accountability. A 10-year-old alone with an iPad and open-internet access will drift to YouTube, because the recommendation and feed-ranking plumbing underneath consumer tech is optimized for that drift, and the ed-tech layer on top doesn't disable it.

- **This is the demand-side confirmation of the thesis in [The Global Edtech Boom Is Fading](/posts/20260424-edu-startups-decline/).** Venture capital left K–12 because outcomes never materialized. Districts are now legislating the rollout out, for the same reason. Venture-backed K–12 needed content delivery to be the bottleneck to justify its valuations, so the category defaulted to that claim even when the evidence was thin. What's left standing is the nonprofit-plus-frontier-API shape (Khan Academy's Khanmigo and similar), which doesn't require the misdiagnosis to make its economics work.
